nameStory: The Atlantic jackknife clam gets its name from its shell's razor-sharp edges and distinctive shape that looks remarkably like an old-fashioned straight razor or jackknife. The streamlined, rectangular shell can actually cut you if you accidentally step on it while beachcombing! It's also called the bamboo clam because of its smooth, segmented appearance.
description: The Atlantic jackknife clam is a large, edible marine clam with an unmistakable long, narrow shell that looks like a folded straight razor. These bivalves live buried in sandy beaches and mudflats along the Atlantic coast, where they use their powerful muscular foot to dig with lightning speed. When threatened, they can burrow deeper faster than most people can dig, making them challenging to catch. They're considered a delicacy and are prized by coastal New Englanders for making homemade clam strips.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Long, narrow, rectangular shell that's much longer than it is wide, resembling a folded straight razor or old jackknife with smooth, clean lines

idTips.label: Sharp Edges
idTips.description: Shell edges are extremely sharp and can cut skin - handle carefully or you'll understand why it's called a razor clam

idTips.label: Breathing Holes
idTips.description: Look for distinctive keyhole-shaped openings in the sand at low tide - these mark where the clams are buried below

idTips.label: Water Jets
idTips.description: When disturbed, shoots small jets of water from its breathing hole as it rapidly digs deeper into the sand

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy shell surface that feels almost porcelain-like to the touch, often with subtle growth lines running parallel to the long edge

idTips.label: Foot Movement
idTips.description: Has a large, powerful white foot that extends from the shell and can be seen rapidly working when the clam is digging

habitat: Atlantic jackknife clams live in sandy beaches, mudflats, and sandy-bottom areas in bays and estuaries throughout New England's coast. You'll find them in both intertidal zones (areas covered and uncovered by tides) and subtidal areas, typically buried 6-12 inches deep in wet sand or mud. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are common in protected coastal waters rather than exposed ocean beaches.

seasonality.spring: Clams become more active as water temperatures warm, making their breathing holes more visible. This is when they begin their most active feeding period.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for finding jackknife clams - breathing holes are most obvious at low tide, and this is when most recreational clamming occurs in coastal Massachusetts towns.
seasonality.fall: Clams remain active but may dig slightly deeper as temperatures drop. Still a good time for observation at low tide.
seasonality.winter: Clams are less active and may burrow deeper, making breathing holes less obvious, though they can still be found during winter low tides.

funFact: These clams are so incredibly fast at digging that MIT engineers have studied them using repurposed ant farms and glass beads to understand their burrowing mechanics - they can disappear into sand faster than a human can dig, even when using tools!
confusionNotes: Atlantic jackknife clams are sometimes confused with other "razor clams" like the Pacific razor clam, but the Atlantic species is found only on the East Coast. Remember: if you're in New England and see a long, narrow clam shell that looks like a straight razor, it's the Atlantic jackknife - no other local clam has this distinctive shape.
contextualKnowledge: The name "razor clam" can be confusing because it refers to several different species on different coasts - the Pacific razor clam is a completely different species. When New Englanders say "razor clam," they're talking about the Atlantic jackknife, but always check local names since some areas may use the terms differently.
compareHints: Since there are no other Ensis species in New England waters, compare the Atlantic jackknife to other local clams - it's the only one with this extremely long, narrow, razor-like shape. Other New England clams like quahogs or steamers are much rounder or oval-shaped. The jackknife's streamlined rectangular shell is absolutely unique among local bivalves.
